Python 3.10.18. Installed deps: gmpy2 2.2.1, numpy 2.2.6, pycryptodome 3.23.0 (importable as `Crypto`), click 8.2.1, nose 1.3.7, pytest 8.3.3. Other agents are concurrently writing OTHER files of the same project — you must ONLY create the files assigned to you below; do not touch any other file, do not create a venv, do not pip-install anything.

Reference semantics (the real phe 1.5.0 — reimplement it faithfully from this description and your own knowledge):

- phe/util.py: `HAVE_GMP` (True if `import gmpy2` succeeds), `HAVE_CRYPTO` (True if `from Crypto.Util import number` succeeds). `powmod(a,b,c)` uses gmpy2.powmod when available, else builtin pow(a,b,c). `mulmod(a,b,c)`, `invert(a,b)` (modular inverse via extended Euclid; gmpy2.invert when available), `getprimeover(N)` (random N-bit prime; uses Crypto's number.getPrime(N) when HAVE_CRYPTO else fallback generating random N-bit odd candidates and testing with is_prime), `isqrt(n)` (math.isqrt ok), `improved_i_sqrt(n)` (bitwise binary-search integer sqrt; asserts n>=0; returns floor sqrt), `extended_euclidean_algorithm(a,b)` returning (gcd, s, t) with gcd = s*a + t*b, `miller_rabin(n, a)` (single-round MR with witness a; False for composite), `is_prime(n, mr_rounds=25)` (n<=1 or negative -> False; trial-divide by first_primes; then Miller-Rabin rounds), `first_primes` (list of the first 1000 primes; may be generated at import time), `int_to_base64(a)` (assert a>0; minimal big-endian bytes -> base64 string) and `base64_to_int(s)`, `base64url_encode(data)`/`base64url_decode(s)` (urlsafe base64 without padding issues).

- phe/encoding.py: `class EncodedNumber` with class attrs `BASE=16`, `LOG2_BASE=math.log(BASE,2)`. `__init__(self, public_key, encoding, exponent)`; `@classmethod encode(cls, public_key, scalar, precision=None, max_exponent=None)` — ints are encoded with exponent 0 (negative ints as `scalar % public_key.n`); floats: default precision = value's ulp-based precision (abs(scalar) * 2**-53 style), exponent = floor(log(precision, BASE)), bin_flt_exponent etc., int_rep = round(scalar * BASE**-exponent), then reduce exponent if abs(int_rep) too large (must stay < n//3); raise ValueError('Integer needs to be within +/- %d' % max_int) when out of range. `decode()` returns float or int (int when exponent >= 0); handles sign via comparing encoding to n - max_int. `decrease_exponent_to(new_exp)` requires new_exp <= self.exponent else ValueError; multiplies encoding by BASE**(self.exponent - new_exp) mod n; also checks overflow vs max_int.

- phe/paillier.py: `DEFAULT_KEYSIZE = 3072`. `generate_paillier_keypair(private_keyring=None, n_length=DEFAULT_KEYSIZE)` — p = util.getprimeover(n_length // 2), q likewise until n = p*q has n_length bits and p != q (loop regenerating p/q as needed); returns (PaillierPublicKey(n), priv); if private_keyring given, add priv to it. `class PaillierPublicKey`: `__init__(self, n)` sets n, nsquare=n*n, g=n+1, max_int = n // 3 - 1. `encrypt(value, precision=None, r_value=None)` -> EncryptedNumber via EncodedNumber.encode + raw_encrypt; `raw_encrypt(plaintext, r_value=None)` raises TypeError unless isinstance(plaintext, int); if r_value given use it (assert 0 < r_value < n? just use it) else r = self.get_random_lt_n(); returns obfuscated ciphertext: nude_ciphertext = (plaintext % n) * n + 1 mod nsquare... actually standard: (self.n * plaintext + 1) % self.nsquare * powmod(r, n, nsquare) % nsquare. `get_random_lt_n()` uses Crypto.Random.random / random.SystemRandom in [1, n). `__repr__` like `<PaillierPublicKey: 12345...>`, `__eq__`/`__hash__` by n.
  `class PaillierPrivateKey`: `__init__(self, public_key, p, q)` (also accepts being built from totient internally); computes lambda/l etc.; stores p,q, psquare, qsquare, p_inverse = invert(p,q), hp/hq precomputed for CRT fast decryption. `raw_decrypt(ciphertext)` raises TypeError unless int; decrypts via CRT (decrypt mod p^2 and q^2, CRT combine). `decrypt(encrypted_number)` -> float/int via decrypt_encoded().decode(); checks encrypted_number.public_key == self.public_key else ValueError. `decrypt_encoded(encrypted_number, Encoding=None)`. `@staticmethod from_totient(public_key, totient)` — factor totient using isqrt of n - totient + 1 etc. `__eq__`/`__hash__` so that PaillierPrivateKey(pk, 43, 59) == PaillierPrivateKey(pk, 59, 43) (compare public_key and {p,q} unordered, e.g. hash of frozenset or p*q and p+q).
  `class PaillierPrivateKeyring`: holds list; `__init__(private_keys=None)`, `add(private_key)`, `decrypt(encrypted_number)` tries each key (catches ValueError) else raises ValueError('no key of the keyring could decrypt'), `__getitem__`, `__len__`, `__iter__`.
  `class EncryptedNumber`: `__init__(public_key, ciphertext, exponent=0)`. `ciphertext(be_secure=True)` — if be_secure, obfuscate once if `self._is_obfuscated` is False, then return `self._ciphertext`. `obfuscate()` multiplies by r**n mod nsquare with random r, sets _is_obfuscated True. Homomorphic ops: `__add__`/`__radd__` (EncryptedNumber+EncryptedNumber requires same public_key (ValueError otherwise) and aligned exponents via decrease_exponent_to; ciphertext product mod nsquare, exponent min; + plain number encodes it; other types return NotImplemented so Python raises TypeError), `__sub__`/`__rsub__` (subtract = add negated encoding; encrypted - encrypted multiplies by invert of other ciphertext mod nsquare), `__mul__`/`__rmul__` by plain scalar only — EncryptedNumber * EncryptedNumber raises NotImplementedError('Good luck with that...'); scalar multiplication via powmod(ciphertext, encoded_scalar, nsquare), exponent += scalar exponent; negative scalar handled by invert; multiplication by 0 must yield an encryption of 0 (handle encoded 0 specially: fresh raw_encrypt(0)), `__truediv__(scalar)` = multiply by 1/scalar. `decrease_exponent_to(new_exp)`. `__neg__`. `__repr__`.

- phe/__about__.py: `__version__ = "1.5.0"` (plus a few metadata strings like __title__, __author__ "CSIRO's Data61", __license__ "GPLv3").

- phe/__init__.py: re-export so that ALL of these work: `from phe import EncodedNumber, EncryptedNumber, generate_paillier_keypair, PaillierPrivateKey, PaillierPrivateKeyring, PaillierPublicKey, powmod, invert, getprimeover, isqrt, improved_i_sqrt, HAVE_GMP, HAVE_CRYPTO, extended_euclidean_algorithm, miller_rabin, first_primes, is_prime, int_to_base64`, plus `from phe import paillier, util, encoding`, `from phe.command_line import cli`, and `phe.__version__` (or __about__).

Behavioral requirements the hidden test suite checks (make sure these hold):
- generate_paillier_keypair(n_length=8..4096) works; public_key.n.bit_length() >= n_length.
- raw_encrypt(n) decrypts to 0, raw_encrypt(n+1) decrypts to 1; raw_encrypt("123") raises TypeError; raw_decrypt(str) raises TypeError.
- PaillierPublicKey(126869).encrypt(1, r_value=1).ciphertext(False) == 126870.
- encrypt(1e100) raises ValueError.
- Full homomorphic algebra: a+b, a-b, scalar*a, a*scalar, a/scalar, sum([...]) with start=0 int, numpy mean/dot over lists of EncryptedNumber (np.mean divides by int; np.dot multiplies encrypted by plain scalars and adds — make sure EncryptedNumber supports being used with numpy object arrays; numpy 2.x may call __array_ufunc__... simplest: do NOT define __array_ufunc__; np.dot/np.mean on python lists of objects falls back to object arithmetic).
- Overflow wraps mod n: encrypt(1) + encrypt(n-1) decrypts to 0.
- EncodedNumber.encode(pub, -15).encoding == (-15) % n; subclassing EncodedNumber with different BASE/LOG2_BASE works.
- improved_i_sqrt: assert on negative; improved_i_sqrt(10**6) == 1000; matches isqrt.
- int_to_base64(0) raises AssertionError.
- is_prime(17881) True; negatives/0/1 False; miller_rabin(4,2) False, miller_rabin(127,2) True.

Key JSON serialisation convention used by the CLI (relevant only if you write command_line.py): public key JWK dict {"kty": "DAJ", "n": int_to_base64(n), "alg": "PAI-GN1", optionally "kid"}; private key {"kty": "DAJ", "pub": <public jwk>, "p": int_to_base64(p), "q": int_to_base64(q)}; encrypted numbers serialised as a JSON list of {"v": int_to_base64(ciphertext), "e": exponent} pairs.

Your assigned files and task:

DOCS: write the Sphinx documentation tree — /workspace/docs/Makefile (standard sphinx quickstart Makefile), /workspace/docs/conf.py (sphinx config importing phe.__about__ for version — guard the import so it works when phe is importable from the project root via sys.path.insert of '..'), /workspace/docs/index.rst, /workspace/docs/installation.rst, /workspace/docs/usage.rst, /workspace/docs/serialisation.rst, /workspace/docs/cli.rst, /workspace/docs/alternatives.rst, /workspace/docs/caveats.rst, /workspace/docs/compatibility.rst, /workspace/docs/phe.rst (API reference using automodule for phe, phe.paillier, phe.encoding, phe.util, phe.command_line), /workspace/docs/requirements.txt (sphinx etc.), /workspace/docs/_static/Magic-Logo.svg (a simple valid placeholder SVG). Content should accurately document the API described in the shared spec: keygen with default 3072-bit keys, EncodedNumber encoding scheme (BASE 16, exponent), homomorphic add/sub/scalar-mul/div, keyring, CLI pheutil usage, JWK serialisation format, security caveats (no encrypted*encrypted, overflow wraps mod n, float precision), alternatives (other HE libraries), Python version compatibility. Do NOT write outside docs/. Sanity check: every .rst file is non-empty and roughly valid reStructuredText (no need to build sphinx).

Work directly in /workspace. When done, run a quick sanity check on whatever you produced (e.g. import it / run a tiny script — for core modules you can generate a 128-bit keypair, encrypt, add, decrypt; keep key sizes small so it is fast). Report back a compact summary: files written and the result of your sanity check.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a subagent to handle a task. The subagent runs as a same-process loop instance with its own context and wire file. Delegating also keeps the bulk of intermediate file contents out of your own context — you get a conclusion back instead of a pile of dumps.

Writing the prompt:
- The subagent starts with zero context — it has not seen this conversation. Brief it like a colleague who just walked into the room: state the goal, list what you already know, hand over the specifics.
- Lookups (read this file, run that test): put the exact path or command in the prompt. The subagent should not have to search for things you already know.
- Investigations (figure out X, find why Y): give the question, not prescribed steps — fixed steps become dead weight when the premise is wrong.
- Do not delegate understanding. If the task hinges on a file path or line number, find it yourself first and write it into the prompt.

Usage notes:
- When the task continues earlier work a subagent already did, prefer resuming that agent (pass its `resume` id) over spawning a fresh instance — the resumed agent keeps its prior context.
- A subagent's result is only visible to you, not to the user. When the user needs to see what a subagent produced, summarize the relevant parts yourself in your own reply.
- Subagents use a fixed 2-hour timeout. If one times out, resume the same agent instead of starting over.

When NOT to use Agent: skip delegation for trivial work you can do directly — reading a file whose path you already know, searching a small known set of files, or any task that takes only a step or two. Delegation has a context-handoff cost; it pays off only when the task is substantial enough to outweigh it.

Once a subagent is running, leave that scope to it: do not redo its searches or reads in parallel, and do not abandon it midway and finish the job manually. Both undo the context savings the delegation was meant to buy.


When `run_in_background=true`, the subagent runs detached from this turn. The completion arrives in a later turn as a synthetic user-role message containing its result — you do not need to poll, sleep, or check on its progress. Continue with other work or respond to the user. Never fabricate or predict what the result will say.

Default to a foreground subagent (omit `run_in_background`) when your next step needs its result — foreground hands the result straight back. Reach for `run_in_background=true` only when you have other work to do while it runs and do not need its result to proceed. Never launch in the background and then immediately wait on it (with `TaskOutput block=true`, sleeping, or otherwise): that just blocks the turn for no benefit — run it in the foreground instead.


Available agent types (pass via subagent_type):
- plan: Read-only implementation planning and architecture design. Use this agent when the parent agent needs a step-by-step implementation plan, key file identification, and architectural trade-off analysis before code changes are made.
  Tools: Glob, Grep, Read
- agent: Default Kimi Code agent
  Tools: Bash, Glob, Grep, Read, Write, Skill, EnterPlanMode, ExitPlanMode, CreateGoal, GetGoal, SetGoalBudget, UpdateGoal, AgentSwarm, TaskList, TaskOutput, TaskStop, Agent, AskUserQuestion, Edit, TodoList
- coder: General software engineering agent — the only subagent type with file-editing tools; use it for any delegated task that must modify code. Use this agent for non-trivial software engineering work that may require reading files, editing code, running commands, and returning a compact but technically complete summary to the parent agent.
  Tools: Bash, Glob, Grep, Read, Write, Skill, EnterPlanMode, ExitPlanMode, AgentSwarm, TaskList, TaskOutput, TaskStop, Agent, Edit, TodoList
- explore: Fast codebase exploration with prompt-enforced read-only behavior. Fast agent specialized for exploring codebases. Use this when you need to quickly find files by patterns (e.g. "src/**/*.yaml"), search code for keywords (e.g. "database connection"), or answer questions about the codebase (e.g. "how does the auth module work?"). When calling this agent, specify the desired thoroughness level: "quick" for basic searches, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "thorough" for comprehensive analysis across multiple locations and naming conventions. Use this agent for any read-only exploration that will clearly require more than 3 search queries. Prefer launching multiple explore agents concurrently when investigating independent questions.
  Tools: Bash, Glob, Grep, Read

prompt.description: Full task prompt for the subagent

description.description: Short task description (3-5 words) for UI display

subagent_type.description: One of the available agent types (see "Available agent types" in this tool description). Defaults to "coder" when omitted.

resume.description: Optional agent ID to resume instead of creating a new instance. When set, do not also pass subagent_type — the resumed agent keeps its own type, and supplying both is rejected.

run_in_background.description: If true, return immediately without waiting for completion. Prefer false unless the task can run independently and there is a clear benefit to not waiting.

model.description: Which model to run the subagent on: "secondary" = the configured secondary model; "primary" = the main model you are running on (for hard, quality-sensitive tasks). This explicit choice overrides the selected agent type's model_preference; without either, secondary is the default when configured. Only effective when a secondary model is configured; otherwise the subagent inherits your model. Ignored when resuming — resumed subagents keep their own model.

tools.name: AgentSwarm
tools.description:
Launch multiple subagents from one prompt template, existing agent resumes, or both.

Use AgentSwarm when many subagents should run the same kind of task over different inputs. The placeholder is exactly `{{item}}`. For example, with `prompt_template` set to `Review {{item}} for likely regressions.` and `items` set to `["src/a.ts", "src/b.ts"]`, AgentSwarm launches two new subagents with those two concrete prompts. For a few differently-shaped tasks, make separate `Agent` calls in one message instead.

Use `resume_agent_ids` to continue subagents that already exist from earlier work, such as ones that failed or timed out: map each agent id to the prompt for that resumed subagent (usually `continue` if no extra information is needed). You may combine `resume_agent_ids` with `items` in the same call to resume existing subagents and launch new ones. Do not duplicate resumed work in `items`.

Each of these is enforced — a violation is rejected before any subagent starts: provide at least 2 `items` unless you pass `resume_agent_ids`; whenever `items` are present, `prompt_template` is required and must contain `{{item}}`; and the filled-in prompts must be distinct (two items that expand to the same prompt are rejected).

Use enough subagents to keep the work focused and parallel. AgentSwarm supports up to 128 subagents, and launches are queued automatically, so it is safe to split large tasks into many clear, independent items.

If `AgentSwarm` is called, that call must be the only tool call in the response.

description.description: Short description for the whole swarm.

subagent_type.description: Subagent type used for every new subagent spawned from items; defaults to coder when omitted. Resumed subagents always keep their original type, so passing subagent_type together with resume_agent_ids is allowed — it only affects the item-based spawns.

prompt_template.description: Prompt template for each subagent. The {{item}} placeholder is replaced with each item value.

items.description: Values used to fill {{item}}. Each item launches one new subagent.

resume_agent_ids.description: Map of existing subagent agent_id to the prompt used to resume that subagent. These resumed subagents are launched before new item-based subagents.

model.description: Which model to run the item-spawned subagents on: "secondary" = the configured secondary model; "primary" = the main model you are running on (for hard, quality-sensitive tasks). This explicit choice overrides the selected agent type's model_preference; without either, secondary is the default when configured. Only effective when a secondary model is configured; otherwise subagents inherit your model. Resumed subagents always keep their own model.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Execute a `bash` command. Use this for shell semantics — pipes, env, processes, git, package managers, build/test runners, anything genuinely interactive or multi-step.

**Translate these to a dedicated tool instead:**
- `cat` / `head` / `tail` (known path) → `Read`
- `sed` / `awk` (in-place edit) → `Edit`
- `echo > file` / `cat <<EOF` → `Write`
- `find` / recursive `ls` to locate files by name pattern → `Glob` (plain `ls <known-directory>` is fine for listing a directory)
- `grep` / `rg` (search file contents) → `Grep`
- `echo` / `printf` (talk to the user) → just output text directly

The dedicated tools render in the per-tool permission UI and keep raw stdout out of the conversation; that is why they are worth reaching for whenever one fits.

**Output:**
The stdout and stderr will be combined and returned as a string. The output may be truncated if it is too long. If the command exits non-zero, the output ends with a `Command failed with exit code: N` line; a command killed by its timeout or interrupted by the user ends with its own message instead.

If `run_in_background=true`, the command will be started as a background task and this tool will return a task ID instead of waiting for command completion. When doing that, you must provide a short `description`. Background commands default to a 600s timeout and `timeout` is capped at 86400s; set `disable_timeout=true` only when the task should run without a timeout. You will be automatically notified when the task completes. After starting one, default to returning control to the user instead of immediately waiting on it. Use `TaskOutput` only for a non-blocking status/output snapshot — do not set `block=true` to wait for a task you just launched, since its completion arrives automatically; reserve `block=true` for when the user explicitly asked you to wait. Use `TaskStop` only if the task must be cancelled. If a human user wants to inspect background tasks themselves, point them to the `/tasks` command, which opens an interactive panel; it has no subcommands.

**Guidelines for safety and security:**
- Each shell tool call will be executed in a fresh shell environment. The shell variables, current working directory changes, and the shell history is not preserved between calls. To run a command in a particular directory, pass the `cwd` argument (or use absolute paths) rather than relying on a `cd` from an earlier call.
- The tool call will return after the command is finished. You shall not use this tool to execute an interactive command or a command that may run forever. For possibly long-running foreground commands, set the `timeout` argument in seconds. Foreground commands default to 60s and allow up to 300s. When a foreground command hits its timeout it is moved to the background instead of being killed, and you will be automatically notified when it completes.
- Avoid using `..` to access files or directories outside of the working directory.
- Avoid modifying files outside of the working directory unless explicitly instructed to do so.
- Never run commands that require superuser privileges unless explicitly instructed to do so.

**Guidelines for efficiency:**
- Use `&&` to chain commands that genuinely depend on each other, e.g. `npm install && npm test`. Independent read-only commands (separate `git show`, `ls`, or status checks) should be issued as separate parallel Bash calls in one response, not chained into a single call — chaining serializes their execution and mixes their output. Do not stitch outputs together with `echo` separators.
- Use `;` to run commands sequentially regardless of success/failure
- Use `||` for conditional execution (run second command only if first fails)
- Use pipe operations (`|`) and redirections (`>`, `>>`) to chain input and output between commands
- Always quote file paths containing spaces with double quotes (e.g., cd "/path with spaces/")
- Compose multi-step logic in a single call with `if` / `case` / `for` / `while` control flows.
- Prefer `run_in_background=true` for long-running builds, tests, watchers, or servers when you need the conversation to continue before the command finishes.

**Commands available:**
The following common command categories are usually available. Availability still depends on the host, so when in doubt run `which <command>` first to confirm a command exists before relying on it.
- Navigation and inspection: `ls`, `pwd`, `cd`, `stat`, `file`, `du`, `df`, `tree`
- File and directory management: `cp`, `mv`, `rm`, `mkdir`, `touch`, `ln`, `chmod`, `chown`
- Text and data processing: `wc`, `sort`, `uniq`, `cut`, `tr`, `diff`, `xargs`
- Archives and compression: `tar`, `gzip`, `gunzip`, `zip`, `unzip`
- Networking and transfer: `curl`, `wget`, `ping`, `ssh`, `scp`
- Version control: `git`; for GitHub-hosted work (PRs, issues, CI runs, API queries) prefer the `gh` CLI when installed — it carries the user's GitHub auth and can return structured JSON
- Process and system: `ps`, `kill`, `top`, `env`, `date`, `uname`, `whoami`
- Language and package toolchains: `node`, `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn`, `python`, `pip` (use whichever the project actually relies on)

cwd.description: The working directory in which to run the command. When omitted, the command runs in the session's working directory.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in seconds for the command to execute. Foreground default 60s, max 300s. Background default 600s, max 86400s. Ignored for background commands when disable_timeout=true.

description.description: A short description for the background task. Required when run_in_background is true.

run_in_background.description: Whether to run the command as a background task.

disable_timeout.description: If true, do not apply a timeout to the command. Only applies when run_in_background is true.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Perform exact replacements in existing files.

- Edit is mandatory for every incremental change, especially small edits. DO NOT use Write or Bash `sed`.
- Read the target file before every Edit. DO NOT call Edit from memory, stale context, or a guessed `old_string`.
- Take `old_string` and `new_string` from the Read output view.
- Drop the line-number prefix and tab; match only file content.
- `old_string` must be unique unless `replace_all` is set.
- If `old_string` is ambiguous, add surrounding context. Use `replace_all` only when every occurrence should change — for example, renaming a symbol throughout the file.
- Multiple Edit calls may run in one response only when they do not target the same file.
- DO NOT issue consecutive Edit calls on the same file. A previous Edit can invalidate a later Edit's `old_string`, causing `old_string not found`. Read the file again before the next Edit.
- A write lock serializes same-file edits in response order, but serialization does not make stale `old_string` valid.
- For pure CRLF files, Read shows LF; use LF in `old_string` and `new_string`, and Edit writes CRLF back.
- For mixed endings or lone carriage returns, Read shows carriage returns as \r; include actual \r escapes in those positions.

path.description: Path to the text file to edit. Relative paths resolve against the working directory; a path outside the working directory must be absolute.

old_string.description: Exact content to replace from the Read output view, without the line-number prefix. Use LF for pure CRLF files; use actual \r escapes where Read shows \r.

new_string.description: Replacement text in the same Read output view. LF is written back as CRLF only for pure CRLF files.

replace_all.description: Set true only when every occurrence of old_string should be replaced.

tools.name: EnterPlanMode
tools.description:
Use this tool proactively when you're about to start a non-trivial implementation task.
Getting user sign-off on your approach via ExitPlanMode before writing code prevents wasted effort.

Use it when ANY of these conditions apply:

1. New Feature Implementation - e.g. "Add a caching layer to the API"
2. Multiple Valid Approaches - e.g. "Optimize database queries" (indexing vs rewrite vs caching)
3. Code Modifications - e.g. "Refactor auth module to support OAuth"
4. Architectural Decisions - e.g. "Add WebSocket support"
5. Multi-File Changes - involves more than 2-3 files
6. Unclear Requirements - need exploration to understand scope
7. User Preferences Matter - if user input would materially change the implementation approach, use EnterPlanMode to structure the decision

Permission mode notes:
- EnterPlanMode enters plan mode automatically without an approval prompt in all permission modes.
- In yolo and manual modes, ExitPlanMode still presents the plan to the user for approval.
- In auto permission mode, do not use AskUserQuestion; make the best decision from available context.
- In auto permission mode, ExitPlanMode exits plan mode without asking the user.
- Use EnterPlanMode only when planning itself adds value.

When NOT to use:
- Single-line or few-line fixes (typos, obvious bugs, small tweaks)
- User gave very specific, detailed instructions
- Pure research/exploration tasks

Once you are in plan mode, a reminder walks you through the workflow (explore → design → write the plan file → `ExitPlanMode`) and enforces read-only access. For non-trivial tasks where you are unsure of the codebase structure or relevant code paths, use `Agent(subagent_type="explore")` to investigate first when the `Agent` tool is available.

tools.name: ExitPlanMode
tools.description:
Use this tool when you are in plan mode and have finished writing your plan to the plan file and are ready for user approval.

## How This Tool Works
- You should have already written your plan to the plan file specified in the plan mode reminder.
- This tool does NOT take the plan content as a parameter - it reads the plan from the file you wrote.
- The user will see the contents of your plan file when they review it. In auto permission mode, the tool reads the file and exits plan mode without asking the user.

## When to Use
Only use this tool for tasks that require planning implementation steps. For research tasks (searching files, reading code, understanding the codebase), do NOT use this tool.

## What a good plan contains
List specific, verifiable steps grounded in the actual codebase — real files, functions, and commands, in a sensible order. Each step should be concrete enough to act on and to check. Avoid vague filler like "improve performance" or "add tests"; say what to change and where.

## Multiple Approaches
If your plan offers multiple alternative approaches, pass them via the `options` parameter so the user can choose which one to execute — see the `options` parameter for the format, count, and reserved labels. In yolo and manual modes the user sees all options alongside the host's Reject and Revise controls.

## Before Using
- In auto permission mode, do NOT use AskUserQuestion; make the best decision from available context.
- In auto permission mode, this tool exits plan mode without asking the user.
- In yolo and manual modes, this tool still presents the plan to the user for approval.
- If auto permission mode is not active and you have unresolved questions, use AskUserQuestion first.
- If auto permission mode is not active and you have multiple approaches and haven't narrowed down yet, consider using AskUserQuestion first to let the user choose, then write a plan for the chosen approach only.
- Once your plan is finalized, use THIS tool to request approval.
- Do NOT use AskUserQuestion to ask "Is this plan OK?" or "Should I proceed?" - that is exactly what ExitPlanMode does.
- If rejected, revise based on feedback and call ExitPlanMode again.

options.description: When the plan contains multiple alternative approaches, list them here so the user can choose which one to execute. Find files by glob pattern, sorted by modification time (most recent first).

Powered by ripgrep. Respects `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` by default — set `include_ignored` to also match ignored files (e.g. build outputs, `node_modules`). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) are always filtered out. Matches are files only — directories themselves are never listed; to find a directory, glob for a file inside it (e.g. `**/fixtures/**`).

Good patterns:
- `*.ts` — all files matching an extension, at any depth below the search root (a bare pattern without `/` matches recursively)
- `src/*.ts` — files directly inside `src/` (one level, not recursive)
- `src/**/*.ts` — recursive walk with a subdirectory anchor and extension
- `**/*.py` — recursive walk from the search root for an extension
- `*.{ts,tsx}` — brace expansion is supported
- `{src,test}/**/*.ts` — cartesian brace expansion is supported too

Results are capped at the first 100 matching paths. If a search would return more, a truncation marker is appended. Refine the pattern (extension, subdirectory) when 100 is not enough, or call again with a narrower anchor.

Large-directory caveat — avoid recursing into dependency / build output even with an anchor, especially when `include_ignored` is set:
- `node_modules/**/*.js`, `.venv/**/*.py`, `__pycache__/**`, `target/**` can produce thousands of results that truncate at the match cap and waste context. Prefer specific subpaths like `node_modules/react/src/**/*.js`.

python-paillier documentation
=============================

**python-paillier** (the ``phe`` package) is a Python 3 library for
Partially Homomorphic Encryption using the Paillier cryptosystem.

The homomorphic properties of the Paillier crypto system are:

- Encrypted numbers can be **added** to other encrypted numbers.
- Encrypted numbers can be **multiplied** by a non-encrypted scalar.
- Encrypted numbers can be **added** to a non-encrypted scalar.
- Encrypted numbers can be **divided** by a non-encrypted scalar.

.. toctree::
   :maxdepth: 2
   :caption: Contents:

   installation
   usage
   serialisation
   cli
   caveats
   alternatives
   compatibility
   phe

Indices and tables
==================

* :ref:`genindex`
* :ref:`modindex`
* :ref:`search`

Installation
============

Using pip
---------

Install from PyPI::

    pip install phe

Or, to build and install from a source checkout::

    pip install -e .

Dependencies
------------

The library requires Python 3 (see :doc:`compatibility` for supported
versions) and has the following optional dependencies, which are used
automatically when importable:

- `gmpy2 <https://github.com/aleaxit/gmpy>`_ — speeds up modular
  arithmetic (``powmod``, ``invert``).  Detected at import time and
  exposed as ``phe.util.HAVE_GMP``.
- `pycryptodome <https://www.pycryptodome.org>`_ — used for prime
  generation (``Crypto.Util.number.getPrime``) and secure random
  number generation.  Detected at import time and exposed as
  ``phe.util.HAVE_CRYPTO``.

Both are strongly recommended: prime generation without pycryptodome
falls back to a pure-Python search using Miller-Rabin primality
testing, which is considerably slower for the default 3072-bit keys.

Building the documentation
--------------------------

The documentation is built with `Sphinx <https://www.sphinx-doc.org>`_::

    pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
    cd docs
    make html

The rendered documentation will be in ``docs/_build/html``.

Usage
=====

Key generation
--------------

Generate a keypair with the default key size (3072 bits)::

    >>> from phe import paillier
    >>> public_key, private_key = paillier.generate_paillier_keypair()

For faster (but less secure) keys during testing, pass ``n_length``::

    >>> public_key, private_key = paillier.generate_paillier_keypair(n_length=128)

Key generation proceeds by drawing two random primes ``p`` and ``q``
of ``n_length // 2`` bits each, repeating until ``n = p * q`` has
exactly ``n_length`` bits and ``p != q``.

You may pass a :class:`~phe.paillier.PaillierPrivateKeyring` to collect
every private key you generate::

    >>> keyring = paillier.PaillierPrivateKeyring()
    >>> public_key, private_key = paillier.generate_paillier_keypair(keyring)

Encryption and decryption
-------------------------

::

    >>> secret_number_list = [3.141592653, 300, -4.6e-12]
    >>> encrypted_number_list = [public_key.encrypt(x) for x in secret_number_list]
    >>> [private_key.decrypt(x) for x in encrypted_number_list]
    [3.141592653, 300, -4.6e-12]

Homomorphic operations
----------------------

Encrypted numbers support addition, subtraction, scalar multiplication
and scalar division::

    >>> a, b, c = encrypted_number_list
    >>> private_key.decrypt(a + b)      # encrypted + encrypted
    303.141592653
    >>> private_key.decrypt(a - 5)      # encrypted - scalar
    -1.8584073469999999
    >>> private_key.decrypt(b * 0.1)    # encrypted * scalar
    30.0
    >>> private_key.decrypt(c / -10)    # encrypted / scalar
    4.6e-13

Because the encrypted values carry their encoding exponent, ``a + b``
works even when the operands were encoded at different precisions; the
library transparently lowers the higher exponent.

Built-in ``sum`` and numpy also work on lists of encrypted numbers::

    >>> from phe import paillier
    >>> import numpy as np
    >>> private_key.decrypt(sum(encrypted_number_list))
    303.14159265299997
    >>> private_key.decrypt(np.mean(encrypted_number_list))
    101.047197551

Note what is *not* supported: multiplying two encrypted numbers raises
``NotImplementedError``.  See :doc:`caveats`.

Keyrings
--------

A :class:`~phe.paillier.PaillierPrivateKeyring` holds multiple private
keys and tries each in turn when decrypting::

    >>> keyring = paillier.PaillierPrivateKeyring()
    >>> keyring.add(private_key)
    >>> keyring.decrypt(a)
    3.141592653

If no key in the ring matches the ciphertext, ``ValueError`` is raised.
Keyrings support indexing, ``len()`` and iteration.

The encoding scheme
-------------------

Paillier encrypts integers modulo ``n``.  To support floats and signed
values, :class:`~phe.encoding.EncodedNumber` maps a scalar to an
integer encoding in ``[0, n)`` together with an exponent (base 16 by
default, ``EncodedNumber.BASE``):

- Integers are encoded with exponent 0; negative integers are encoded
  as ``scalar % n``.
- Floats are encoded as ``round(scalar * BASE ** -exponent)`` with an
  exponent derived from the requested (or default ulp-based) precision.
- ``max_int = n // 3 - 1`` is the largest absolute value that can be
  represented; values between ``max_int`` and ``n - max_int`` are
  reserved so that overflow of positive and negative numbers can be
  detected.  Values out of range raise ``ValueError``.

Decoding returns an ``int`` when the exponent is non-negative,
otherwise a ``float``.

Serialisation
=============

Keys and encrypted numbers can be serialised to JSON so they can be
shared between parties.  The convention used by the library (and by
the :doc:`command line tool <cli>`) is based on JSON Web Keys (JWK).

Public keys
-----------

A :class:`~phe.paillier.PaillierPublicKey` is represented as a JWK-like
dictionary::

    {"kty": "DAJ", "n": "<base64 of n>", "alg": "PAI-GN1", "kid": "optional key id"}

where ``<base64 of n>`` is produced by
:func:`phe.util.int_to_base64` — the modulus ``n`` as minimal
big-endian bytes, base64-encoded.

Example::

    import json
    from phe.util import int_to_base64, base64_to_int
    from phe.paillier import PaillierPublicKey

    # Serialise
    jwk = {"kty": "DAJ", "alg": "PAI-GN1", "n": int_to_base64(public_key.n)}
    blob = json.dumps(jwk)

    # Deserialise
    data = json.loads(blob)
    assert data["kty"] == "DAJ"
    public_key = PaillierPublicKey(n=base64_to_int(data["n"]))

Private keys
------------

A :class:`~phe.paillier.PaillierPrivateKey` embeds the public JWK plus
the two prime factors::

    {"kty": "DAJ", "pub": <public jwk>, "p": "<base64 of p>", "q": "<base64 of q>"}

Example::

    private_jwk = {
        "kty": "DAJ",
        "kid": "optional key id",
        "pub": public_jwk,
        "p": int_to_base64(private_key.p),
        "q": int_to_base64(private_key.q),
    }

    # Deserialise
    pub = PaillierPublicKey(n=base64_to_int(private_jwk["pub"]["n"]))
    priv = paillier.PaillierPrivateKey(
        pub, p=base64_to_int(private_jwk["p"]), q=base64_to_int(private_jwk["q"]))

.. warning::

   A serialised private key grants full decryption capability to anyone
   who obtains it.  Store and transmit it with the same care you would
   give any other private key material.

Encrypted numbers
-----------------

Encrypted numbers are serialised as a JSON list of objects holding the
ciphertext and the encoding exponent::

    [{"v": "<base64 of ciphertext>", "e": <exponent>}, ...]

Example::

    serialised = json.dumps([
        {"v": int_to_base64(x.ciphertext()), "e": x.exponent}
        for x in encrypted_number_list
    ])

    # Deserialise
    received = json.loads(serialised)
    encrypted = [
        paillier.EncryptedNumber(public_key, base64_to_int(d["v"]), d["e"])
        for d in received
    ]

Call ``ciphertext()`` (with its default ``be_secure=True``) rather than
reading the raw attribute: it obfuscates the ciphertext with a fresh
random factor before it leaves your control.

Command line usage
==================

Installing the package provides the ``pheutil`` command line tool
(defined in ``phe.command_line``), which supports key generation,
encryption and extraction of a public key from a private key.

Running ``pheutil --help`` lists the available commands::

    $ pheutil --help
    Usage: pheutil [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

      CLI for interacting with phe's paillier crypto system.

    Commands:
      extract  Extract the public key from a private key.
      genpkey  Generate a paillier private key.
      encrypt  Encrypt a number with the given public key.

Generating a private key
------------------------

::

    pheutil genpkey --keysize 2048 privatekey.json

The generated private key is written as JSON in the JWK-based format
described in :doc:`serialisation`.  ``--keysize`` defaults to 3072.

You can also supply a ``--id`` to record a ``kid`` field in the key.

Extracting a public key
-----------------------

::

    pheutil extract privatekey.json publickey.json

This writes a public key JWK (``{"kty": "DAJ", "n": ..., "alg":
"PAI-GN1"}``) that can be shared with anyone who needs to encrypt
data for you.

Encrypting data
---------------

``pheutil encrypt`` reads a public key and one or more plaintext values,
and writes a JSON list of encrypted numbers (``{"v": ciphertext, "e":
exponent}`` objects)::

    pheutil encrypt publickey.json 3.1415 100 -0.2
    pheutil encrypt publickey.json --output encrypted.json 3.1415 100

Values are parsed as floats, so integers should be written plainly and
fractional numbers with a decimal point.  The output can be decrypted
in Python::

    import json
    from phe import paillier
    from phe.util import base64_to_int

    with open("encrypted.json") as f:
        data = json.load(f)
    encrypted = [paillier.EncryptedNumber(public_key,
                                          base64_to_int(d["v"]), d["e"])
                 for d in data]
    print([private_key.decrypt(x) for x in encrypted])

Caveats
=======

Partial, not full, homomorphism
-------------------------------

Paillier is an *additively* homomorphic scheme.  You can add encrypted
numbers and multiply them by plaintext scalars, but you **cannot
multiply two encrypted numbers together** — attempting to do so raises
``NotImplementedError``::

    >>> enc_a * enc_b
    Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
    NotImplementedError: Good luck with that...

This also means numpy operations that reduce via multiplication of
encrypted operands (e.g. ``np.prod``) will not work.

Overflow wraps modulo n
-----------------------

Arithmetic on encrypted numbers is performed modulo the public modulus
``n``.  If the true result of a computation exceeds ``max_int`` (=
``n // 3 - 1``) it silently wraps around::

    >>> huge = public_key.encrypt(public_key.max_int)
    >>> private_key.decrypt(huge + huge)   # not 2 * max_int!

Likewise, adding ciphertexts whose plaintexts sum to ``n`` yields an
encryption of 0.  Choose a key size large enough that intermediate
results stay within ``+/- max_int``, and treat the sign of any
decrypted value near ``n`` as untrustworthy.

Float precision
---------------

Floats are encoded with a fixed-point exponent scheme (base 16).
The default precision is derived from the float's unit in the last
place (roughly ``abs(scalar) * 2**-53``), and adding numbers with
different exponents lowers the result to the coarser exponent.  Very
large magnitudes (e.g. ``1e100``) cannot be represented within
``max_int`` and raise ``ValueError`` at encryption time; very small
values lose resolution.  Repeated operations accumulate rounding just
as with ordinary floating point.

Semantic security vs. malleability
----------------------------------

``EncryptedNumber.ciphertext()`` obfuscates the ciphertext (by
multiplying in a fresh random encryption of zero) before returning it,
so repeated encryptions of the same value look different.  However the
scheme is *malleable by design*: anyone holding the public key can
homomorphically alter a ciphertext.  Do not use ciphertexts as
authentic evidence of a value.

Key security
------------

- The default key size is 3072 bits.  Smaller sizes (``n_length`` below
  2048) are only suitable for testing.
- Protect private keys and any JSON serialisation of them — possession
  of ``p`` and ``q`` is equivalent to possession of the private key.
- Randomness for encryption comes from ``Crypto.Random`` when
  pycryptodome is installed, else ``random.SystemRandom``.

Alternatives
============

python-paillier implements the additively homomorphic Paillier scheme.
If your application needs richer operations (in particular,
multiplication of two encrypted values) or better performance, consider
one of these projects:

- `Microsoft SEAL <https://github.com/Microsoft/SEAL>`_ — C++
  implementation of the BFV and CKKS (fully/leveled homomorphic)
  schemes, with Python bindings via
  `seal-python <https://github.com/Huelse/SEAL-Python>`_ or
  `pyseal <https://github.com/Lab41/PySEAL>`_.
- `PALISADE <https://gitlab.com/palisade/palisade-release>`_ /
  `OpenFHE <https://github.com/openfheorg/openfhe-development>`_ —
  general-purpose lattice cryptography libraries supporting BFV, BGV
  and CKKS.
- `HElib <https://github.com/homenc/HElib>`_ — IBM's implementation of
  the BGV and CKKS schemes.
- `TFHE <https://github.com/tfhe/tfhe>`_ — fast homomorphic operations
  on individual bits / booleans.
- `Pyfhel <https://github.com/ibarrond/Pyfhel>`_ — "Python for
  Homomorphic Encryption Libraries", wrapping SEAL and PALISADE.
- `TenSEAL <https://github.com/OpenMined/TenSEAL>`_ — tensor-oriented
  homomorphic encryption library built on Microsoft SEAL.
- `Concrete <https://github.com/zama-ai/concrete>`_ — Zama's TFHE-based
  framework with a Python frontend for compiling programs to operate
  on encrypted data.

Within the Paillier family specifically, alternatives include
`python-paillier's <https://github.com/data61/python-paillier>`_ peers
such as `phe (pure python) <https://github.com/data61/python-paillier>`_
variants using different backends and
`paillierlib <https://github.com/n1analytics/paillierlib>`_.

Choose CKKS-based libraries (SEAL, OpenFHE, TenSEAL) when you need
approximate arithmetic on vectors of floats; choose Paillier when you
need simple, exact additive homomorphism with small ciphertexts and
mature, easy-to-audit code.

Compatibility
=============

Python versions
---------------

python-paillier 1.5.0 targets Python 3. It is developed and tested
against Python 3.6 through 3.10, and works on newer 3.x releases.

Python 2 is not supported by this release line; use ``phe`` 1.2.x or
earlier if you are stuck on Python 2.7.

Optional dependency backends
----------------------------

At import time the library detects optional accelerators and exposes
the result as flags in :mod:`phe.util`:

``phe.util.HAVE_GMP``
    ``True`` when `gmpy2 <https://github.com/aleaxit/gmpy>`_ is
    importable.  When present it is used for ``powmod`` and modular
    inversion; otherwise the pure-Python built-ins are used.

``phe.util.HAVE_CRYPTO``
    ``True`` when ``Crypto.Util.number`` (pycryptodome) is importable.
    When present it is used for prime generation and cryptographically
    secure random numbers; otherwise the library falls back to a
    pure-Python prime search (Miller-Rabin based) and
    ``random.SystemRandom``.

All backends implement identical semantics, so code is portable across
environments with or without the optional dependencies — only
performance differs.

Interoperability
----------------

The serialisation format (see :doc:`serialisation`) is stable: keys
and ciphertexts produced by one version of the library can be consumed
by another, and the JWK-based format is shared with the N1 Analytics
ecosystem of Paillier tooling.
